# Social Networks in R

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1. Import libraries

```{r warning=FALSE}
library(igraph)  # network creation + analysis
library(ggraph)  # network plotting (ggplot-style)
library(ggplot2) # underlying plotting system
```

### 2. Set seed for randomization

Makes layout and community detection reproducible.

```{r}
set.seed(1111)
```

### 3. Read the graph

This network is undirected, named, and weighted. It has 11 nodes (actors), and 14 edges (co-acting relationships). The node attributes are `wonOscar` (numeric), `name`). The edge attributes are `weight` (numeric).

```{r}

# Read graphml file from GitHub
actors <- read_graph("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DACSS-Anjelica/Homework_2/main/hollywood.graphml", format = "graphml")

# Print a summary of the contents of the graph structure
summary(actors)
```

### 3. Network Visualization

```{r warning=FALSE}
# Plot the network using ggraph
ggraph(graph = actors) +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(
      label = weight
    ),
    alpha = 0.5,
    label_size = 2.5,
    angle_calc = "along"
  ) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name, color = as.factor(wonOscar)), repel = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue")) +
  theme_graph()
```

### 4. Compute node central measures:

Computes eigenvector, closeness, and betweenness centrality and assembles into a dataframe.

```{r}
# Eigenvector Centrality
eigen <- eigen_centrality(actors)$vector

# Closeness
close <- closeness(actors, normalized = TRUE)

#Betweeness
betw  <- betweenness(actors, normalized = TRUE)

# Combines centrality measures into single dataframe for easy interpretation
DFCentrality <- data.frame(
  person = V(actors)$name,
  Eigenvector = eigen,
  Closeness = close,
  Betweenness = betw,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Review the table
head(DFCentrality)
```

### Correlation plot with measures

These centrality measures point to different kinds of acting relationships in the network. Eigenvector centrality is strongly negatively related to closeness (−0.684), which suggests that actors who work with very well-connected people are not always the ones who are closest to everyone else overall. Closeness and betweenness, however, are strongly positively related (0.766), meaning that actors who are easier to reach in the network often also help connect different groups of actors. The weaker negative relationship between eigenvector centrality and betweenness (−0.245) shows that being part of a tight circle of frequent collaborators is not the same as acting as a bridge between separate groups.

```{r}

# Computes correlation matrix for the three centrality measures
cor_mat <- cor(DFCentrality[, c("Eigenvector","Closeness","Betweenness")])

# Prints rounded correlations for readability
print(round(cor_mat, 3))
```

```{r}
# Converts correlation matrix into long format
cor_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_mat))
names(cor_df) <- c("Measure1","Measure2","Correlation")

# Plots correlation matrix as a heatmap with values
ggplot(cor_df, aes(Measure1, Measure2, fill = Correlation)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Correlation, 2)), size = 4) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Correlation among centrality measures")
```

## Questions

### Q1. Is it possible communities are present? Support your answer with computations.

The correlation results show that the different centrality measures capture distinct roles within the actor network. Eigenvector centrality is strongly negatively correlated with closeness (−0.68), indicating that actors who are connected to other highly connected actors are not necessarily the ones who are closest to everyone else in the network. Closeness and betweenness are strongly positively correlated (0.77), suggesting that actors who can reach others quickly also tend to serve as important connectors between different parts of the network. The weaker negative correlation between eigenvector centrality and betweenness (−0.25) further highlights that being influential within a tight collaboration group is different from acting as a bridge between groups. Overall, these patterns show that centrality measures reflect different types of importance rather than a single notion of prominence.

```{r}
# Create a random graph with the same number of nodes and similar density as the real network

randomNet <- sample_gnp(vcount(actors), p = edge_density(actors), directed = FALSE)

# Compute global transitivity (clustering coefficient):
t_real <- transitivity(actors, type = "global")
t_rand <- transitivity(randomNet, type = "global")

# Print transitivity values
cat("Transitivity real:", round(t_real, 3), "\n")
cat("Transitivity random:", round(t_rand, 3), "\n")
cat("Ratio real/random:", round(t_real / t_rand, 2), "\n")
```

### Q2: If the presence of communities is possible, compute the communities using Girvan-Newman and Louvain algorithms. Plot the best result.

Modularity also supports the idea that communities are present in the network. Both community detection methods identify clear groupings of actors, with Girvan–Newman producing a slightly higher modularity score (0.420) than Louvain (0.412). For that reason, I selected the Girvan–Newman results. The resulting communities show two main clusters of actors who have worked together more frequently within their groups than with actors outside of them. One cluster is smaller and more tightly connected, while the other is larger with many overlapping collaborations, suggesting that actors tend to form stable collaboration circles rather than working evenly across the entire network.

```{r warning=FALSE}

# Detects communities using Girvan–Newman:
gn <- cluster_edge_betweenness(actors)

# # Detect communities using Louvain:
lv <- cluster_louvain(actors)

# Compute modularity scores to compare community partition quality
mod_gn <- modularity(gn)
mod_lv <- modularity(lv)

# Print modularity results
cat("Girvan-Newman modularity:", round(mod_gn, 3), "\n")
cat("Louvain modularity:", round(mod_lv, 3), "\n")
```

### **Best Method:** Girvan-Newman

```{r}
# Select the best method with higher modularity
best_method <- ifelse(mod_lv >= mod_gn, "Louvain", "Girvan-Newman")
cat("Best method:", best_method, "\n")

# Store the chosen community membership as a node attribute
V(actors)$community <- if (best_method == "Louvain") {
  as.factor(membership(lv))
} else {
  as.factor(membership(gn))
}

# Plot the best method
ggraph(actors, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_node_point(aes(color = community), size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), repel = TRUE, size = 3, family = "sans") +
  theme_graph(base_family = "sans")
```
